claims.text: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Adding approximately 0.1–0.3 at.% boron during alloy processing can cause boron to segregate at interfaces between the lamellar phases.
Boron segregation at internal lamellar boundaries increases boundary cohesion.
Increased boundary cohesion reduces stress concentrations at lamellar interfaces.
Boron segregation reduces the likelihood of microcrack initiation during tensile loading.
Boron provides solid-solution strengthening in the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
A 0.1–0.3 at.% boron addition will increase room-temperature yield strength relative to the boron-free baseline.
A 0.1–0.3 at.% boron addition will increase room-temperature fracture strain relative to the boron-free baseline.
The beneficial effect of boron is confined to a narrow concentration range of approximately 0.1–0.3 at.%.
Boron concentrations above the proposed range may produce brittle boride phases.
The intervention is effective only when processing produces targeted interfacial segregation rather than random boron distribution.
Rapid solidification or suitable thermal treatments can promote interfacial boron segregation while avoiding brittle boride precipitation.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and fracture strain relative to a boron-free control would falsify the predicted combined benefit.
Absence of preferential boron segregation at lamellar boundaries would falsify the proposed segregation-mediated mechanism.
